currentContext.business: MDL designs, builds, repairs, refits and provides lifecycle support for warships, submarines and allied engineering products, operating through its Operations and Technical Division from facilities at Mumbai, Nhava and other operational locations. Its portfolio spans eight product and service lines — warships, submarines, Coast Guard vessels, export commercial vessels, green ships, offshore projects, ship repair and refit, and global submarine lifecycle support — serving the Indian Navy, the Indian Coast Guard, ONGC, the Shipping Corporation of India and international commercial owners. The AR states that, given the strategic and security-sensitive nature of operations and the exemption available in respect of detailed segment reporting, performance is discussed only at a broad operational level rather than as a segment result.

Warships for the Indian Navy: Project P15B Visakhapatnam Class Guided Missile Destroyers (all four delivered ahead of contractual schedule)
Project P17A Nilgiri Class Stealth Frigates (INS Nilgiri, INS Udaygiri, INS Taragiri, INS Mahendragiri)
Destroyers, frigates, corvettes, missile boats and offshore patrol vessels delivered since nationalisation in 1960
Submarines and submarine lifecycle suppo: Project P-75 Scorpene Class conventional submarines built under licence with French collaborator M/s Naval Group (six delivered, including INS Kalvari and INS Vaghsheer)
German SSK Class submarines (INS Shalki, first Indian-built submarine)
R&D programmes for Expendable Underwater Target and Mobile Target Emulator
Global submarine lifecycle support across both SSK and Scorpene technologies
Export commercial vessels: 7,500 DWT Multi-Purpose Hybrid Powered Vessels for Navi Merchants A/S, Denmark (six, with an option for four more)
Green vessels: Methanol Dual Fuel Diesel Electric Platform Supply Vessel (3,000 DWT) for the Shipping Corporation of India — described as India's first
Offshore projects: ONGC Part Replacement of Pipeline Project (PRPP) — subsea pipelines, approx. 44 km
ONGC Discovered Small Field-II — six new wellhead platforms, modification of three platforms, subsea pipe laying approx. 200 km
ONGC PRP 8(a) — subsea pipe laying approx. 59.8 km plus 17.9 km piggyback with modification to existing platforms
Ship repair and refit: Repair, refit, maintenance and modernisation of defence and commercial vessels
Coast Guard vessel refit and guarantee support (ICGS Saksham)

currentContext.expansion: MDL's expansion programme is entirely infrastructure-led and is described as continuous upgradation and modernisation of existing facilities rather than a single named project. NHAVA YARD: development of the Company's land parcel at Nhava, admeasuring approximately 37 acres, is described as one of the most significant capacity expansion initiatives undertaken by the Company. The greenfield shipyard is being developed in a phased manner to support shipbuilding, ship repair and future growth; facilities include Hard Stands, a Jetty, Workshops, Stores, an Administrative Building, provision of LL Cranes and allied services, and will facilitate construction of ships and offshore platforms. The short-term development plan focuses on optimising utilisation of existing infrastructure to support current business opportunities; the long-term plan aims to establish world-class facilities capable of supporting construction, repair and modernisation of larger and more complex vessels and submarines. No completion date is stated. SOUTH YARD ANNEX / ADDITIONAL WATERFRONT INFRASTRUCTURE: development of a newly acquired land parcel of approximately 15 acres adjacent to the existing facilities (adjacent to MPA land) to enable simultaneous construction, outfitting and repair/refit of various types of vessels; on completion the AR states the project 'will enhance the waterfront handling capacity from the existing 80 DWT to 200 DWT, enabling simultaneous execution of multiple projects'. The unit 'DWT' is reproduced exactly as printed. No completion date is stated. FLOATING DRY DOCK: development of a new Floating Dry Dock of 12,000T capacity has been undertaken to handle the dry-docking requirements of future major projects and to improve docking flexibility and support growth in ship repair, maintenance and modernisation. No completion date is stated. CRANES AND YARD WORKS: replacement of the existing eight vintage Level Luffing Cranes with new modernised cranes is being undertaken in a phased manner (the Corporate Overview 'Financial Capital' spread states this programme is 65% complete); a 150 T Level Luffing Crane is being set up at Alcock Yard; a new Fabrication Workshop including stores is being set up at Alcock Yard; a new Caisson Gate is being manufactured for the East Yard Dry Dock to replace the existing gate; replacement of the Kasara Basin Gate is in progress; and infrastructure augmentation is being progressed in the East Yard to undertake pressure hull fabrication for future Submarine projects. FUTURE GREENFIELD SHIPYARD: the Company states it is in dialogue with State Governments (Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh) on both coasts of India to explore the feasibility of setting up a Greenfield Shipyard in line with the Government of India's Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 — a feasibility dialogue, not a sanctioned project. STATED AMBITION: the Value Creation Story spread states the capital expenditure programme includes acquiring adjacent land parcels to construct larger dry docks, 'aiming to nearly double its total shipbuilding and vessel repair capacities'. RUPEE QUANTUM (stated in prose, deliberately NOT placed in capex_disclosed because it does not arrive under a NAMED DISCLOSURE heading): the Corporate Overview 'Financial Capital' chapter states 'Capital expenditure for FY 2025-26 was Rs 471.81 crore, directed entirely at infrastructure modernisation: the phased crane replacement programme (65% complete), Nhava Yard development, the new 12,000T Floating Dry Dock, Alcock Yard infrastructure additions, and South Yard Annex preparation', and separately that MDL invested Rs 236.95 crore in the equity of Colombo Dockyard PLC, with all capex and the CDPLC investment self-funded from operating cashflows. OPERATIONAL CAPEX ADJACENCY: fabrication of two Jackets and Top sides for the ONGC DSF-II project at the Nhava Yard is approaching completion, with four more Jackets and Top sides in progress at Vietnam; ONGC PRP 8(a) pipe-laying is expected to be completed during the next season, spanning 15 October 2026 to 15 May 2027. risks.risk: Project execution risk on long-cycle warship and submarine programmes
risks.note: Warship and submarine construction involves extended execution timelines owing to technological complexity, stringent quality requirements and evolving customer specifications. The MD&A risk table states the potential impact as 'Delays in achievement of project milestones, cost overruns and impact on contractual commitments', mitigated through robust project planning, periodic milestone reviews, management oversight and project monitoring mechanisms. Because revenue is recognised on milestone achievement, execution slippage translates directly into revenue and margin slippage.

risks.risk: Fixed-price contract exposure to cost escalation, inflation and foreign exchange volatility
risks.note: Listed as a Threat in the SWOT and again as Foreign Exchange Risk in the MD&A risk table: 'Cost escalation, inflationary pressures, foreign exchange rates volatility and delays in project execution may adversely affect margins under fixed-price contracts, particularly in projects involving imported equipment, Systems and critical material.' Mitigation is limited to monitoring foreign currency exposure and 'appropriate financial risk management measures' — no hedging policy is described. This is the clearest structural margin risk in the AR.

risks.risk: Dependence on overseas suppliers for select critical systems, with geopolitical and sanctions exposure
risks.note: Disclosed as both a Weakness and a named risk row: certain critical systems, sensors, propulsion equipment and specialised components continue to be sourced from overseas suppliers, exposing the Company to 'geopolitical developments, sanctions and international supply chain disruptions'. Mitigation is enhanced localisation, indigenous vendor development and strategic sourcing — the same indigenisation programme the Company presents as a strength, meaning the moat and the risk are two views of one unfinished transition (indigenous content is 75% in P17A, so a residual quarter of content remains exposed).

risks.risk: Order book and customer concentration — a single sovereign customer group and lumpy programme awards
risks.note: The MD&A risk table names 'Order Book and Revenue Risk: Delays, deferment or modification of customer programmes impacting revenue visibility', mitigated by diversification, expansion into lifecycle support and exploration of export markets. Structurally, MDL's demand comes almost entirely from the Indian Navy, the Indian Coast Guard and ONGC, all Government-linked, with the Ministry of Defence disclosed as a Government-related party with which significant transactions are carried out. The order book itself fell from Rs 32,260 crore at 31 March 2025 to Rs 20,535 crore at 31 March 2026 (from the strategy_outlook bundle), so replenishment risk is live rather than theoretical.

risks.risk: Dependence on defence procurement policy and budgetary allocation
risks.note: The MD&A cautionary statement enumerates 'changes in Government policies relating to defence procurement, budgetary allocations, geopolitical developments' as factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. Regulatory and Compliance Risk is separately tabled with the potential impact of 'Financial, legal and reputational exposure arising from changes in laws, regulations and contractual obligations', and the SWOT Threats add that changes in defence procurement procedures, taxation, regulatory frameworks or budgetary priorities may influence business opportunities and operational performance.

risks.risk: Human capital risk — high dependency on scarce specialised technical skills
risks.note: Disclosed as a Weakness ('Construction of sophisticated defence platforms requires a highly skilled workforce possessing specialised technical competencies') and as a tabled risk ('Availability and retention of specialised technical talent required for complex projects'), mitigated through talent development, succession planning, capability enhancement and employee engagement. No attrition rate or headcount figure is disclosed anywhere in the routed text, so the risk cannot be sized.

risks.risk: Waterfront constraints, siltation and infrastructure/operational disruption
risks.note: A shipyard-specific structural constraint disclosed as a Weakness: 'The Company's operations require periodic dredging and maintenance of waterfront facilities. Such activities involve recurring expenditure and operational planning challenges.' The tabled Infrastructure and Operational Risk adds 'Operational disruptions arising from facility constraints, waterfront maintenance requirements and infrastructure-related challenges', mitigated by continuous infrastructure upgrades, preventive maintenance and capacity augmentation — which is precisely why the capex programme (Nhava, South Yard Annex, floating dry dock, basin and caisson gates) is maintenance-heavy rather than purely growth capex.

risks.risk: Governance risk — Board composition is outside the Company's control and has already triggered exchange penalties
risks.note: Not labelled a risk by the Company, but structurally one: the power to appoint all Directors vests with the President of India acting through the Ministry of Defence, and the Company disclosed that it received notices from NSE and BSE imposing fines for failure to maintain the requisite number of Board members under Regulation 17(1) of SEBI (LODR), stating that compliance 'was beyond the control of the Company'. Fines were waived till 31 October 2024 and reversed to 31 December 2024, with a waiver still to be sought for the remaining period. Four Independent Directors ceased between January and April 2026, leaving one Independent Director on the Corporate Information page, so recurrence risk is immediate. Back-filled from the governance_entities bundle, which routes this disclosure.

one-line thesis: MDL delivered record FY25 revenue of Rs.11,432cr and PAT of Rs.2,325cr driven by P-15B and P-75 deliveries, but Q4 EBITDA margin collapsed to 13.7% due to Rs.532cr loss provisions on Coast Guard and Denmark FPV contracts; the imminent signing of P-75(AS) and P-75(I) submarine contracts (expected by June 2025) will catapult order book from Rs.32,000cr to over Rs.1.25 lakh cr, transforming MDL into India’s sole strategic submarine hub with long-term margin upside.
financial scorecard: revenue: +20% YoY to Rs.11,432cr; EBITDA/margin: 28.24% (FY25) but Q4 dropped to 13.74% due to Rs.532cr provision; PAT (rptd): Rs.2,325cr; PAT (normalized): ~Rs.2,857cr (add back Rs.532cr provision); order book: Rs.32,260cr (pre-signing); net debt: Net cash position of Rs.11,000-12,000cr (Rs.6,000cr margin money, Rs.6,000cr advances)
guidance: revenue growth: 8-10% CAGR; margin: 15% PBT guidance (prudent); order inflow: >Rs.1.25 lakh cr expected by FY26 end; capex/commissioning: Rs.4,000cr CAPEX for Nhava yard and SSA facility, commissioning expected FY27-28
order book & pipeline: Rs.32,260cr (pre-P-75(AS)/P-75(I)); includes P-15B (Rs.13,493cr), P-17A (Rs.13,493cr), P-75 Kalvari (Rs.2,400cr), ONGC (Rs.6,500cr), Denmark FPV (Rs.1,800cr), Coast Guard FPV (Rs.1,700cr); post-signing expected to exceed Rs.1.25 lakh cr
segment / subsidiary detail: Warships: P-15B (delivered), P-17A (4 ships, 3 to deliver by FY26); Submarines: P-75 Kalvari (completed), P-75(AS) (30-40k cr, signing expected June 2025), P-75(I) (6 subs, commercial negotiations ongoing); Commercial: 6 FPVs for Coast Guard (Rs.1,700cr), 1 multipurpose vessel for Europe (Rs.715cr); Ship Repair: Wet basin/dry dock used; AIP/MRLC upgrades contributing Rs.4,000cr revenue
growth verticals / optionality: P-17B frigates (Rs.70,000cr RFP expected soon), MCMV (Rs.44,000cr RFP in pipeline), export expansion via Denmark FPV optional 4 ships, potential commercial shipbuilding cluster tie-ups, submarine hub for regional exports
margins & cost dynamics: Q4 EBITDA margin dropped to 13.74% due to Rs.532cr provision on Denmark and Coast Guard FPV contracts (cost escalation from 2022-23 bid prices); fixed-price contracts dominate (2/3 of order book); raw material costs locked at bid stage; subcontracting costs up due to 27-ship parallel build and outsourcing; long-term margin upside from P-75(AS)/P-75(I) economies of scale
capex / expansion: Rs.4,000cr allocated for Nhava yard and SSA (submarine section assembly) facility; land acquired from port for small ship expansion; CAPEX funded internally (no debt planned); commissioning expected FY27-28
capital allocation: Strong net cash position (Rs.11,000-12,000cr); no debt planned; focus on internal funding of CAPEX; potential for dividend payout or strategic M&A in ship repair/commercial segment
risks & watch-items: Delays in P-75(AS)/P-75(I) contract signing; cost overruns in fixed-price contracts; supply chain disruptions for imported components; geopolitical delays in RFPs (P-17B, MCMV); labor and skill shortages; provision reversals uncertain
management quality / tone: Confident, strategic, and disciplined; underpromised 15% PBT margin despite FY25’s 27.2% to manage expectations; emphasized indigenous content (60%+ in P-75(I)); proactive on diversification (ONGC, Europe); transparent on provisions and CAPEX; clear timeline for submarine contract signing
non-obvious takeaways: Rs.3,700cr P-15B and Rs.2,700cr P-75 backlog are not revenue but guarantee/liability provisions; Rs.4,000cr ship repair revenue includes AIP/MRLC upgrades (not dry dock repairs); Rs.6,500cr ONGC order is offshore support vessel (not oil rigs); submarine CAPEX is for indigenous assembly, not nuclear

themes.title: Naval shipbuilding & maritime
themes.need: A multi-decade naval order book and indigenous warship/submarine build, plus the naval-equipment supply chain (HVAC/chillers, mechanical seals, marine gearing) and maritime services, underpin the theme. GRSE carries a large RFP pipeline (~INR1.5 lakh cr referenced); SHREE REFRIGERATIONS 544458 supplies naval HVAC; SEALMATIC 543782 naval/submarine seals; ELECON defence-marine gearing; KMEW/SEAMECLTD/DREDGECORP maritime services.
themes.driver: Fresh MoD warship/submarine orders + naval-equipment indigenization inflow; maritime-infra/offshore contract wins.

one_liner.body: Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited is a Navratna Defence Public Sector Undertaking under the administrative control of the Ministry of Defence and India's leading shipyard for construction, repair, refit, modernisation and lifecycle support of warships and submarines — the only Indian shipyard to …

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: MDL designs, builds, repairs, refits and provides lifecycle support for warships, submarines and allied engineering products, operating through its Operations and Technical Division from facilities at Mumbai, Nhava and other operational locations. Its portfolio spans eight product and service lines — warships, submarines, Coast Guard vessels, export commercial vessels, green ships, offshore projects, ship repair and refit, and global submarine lifecycle support — serving the Indian Navy, the Indian Coast Guard, ONGC, the Shipping Corporation of India and international commercial owners. The AR states that, given the strategic and security-sensitive nature of operations and the exemption available in respect of detailed segment reporting, performance is discussed only at a broad operational level rather than as a segment result.

group_structure.title: Group structure (profile)
group_structure.body:
- Colombo Dockyard PLC (CDPLC), Sri Lanka — subsidiary: 51% held by MDL; became a subsidiary during FY 2025-26 following acquisition of a controlling stake, date of acquisition stated as 19.01.2026 in Form AOC-1. A Sri Lankan public limited company incorporated in 1974 and listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange, with operations spanning shipbuilding and ship repair. Reporting currency LKR. MDL's Chairman & Managing Director is also Chairman of CDPLC. Described as MDL's first international acquisition in its 250-year history.
- Dockyard General Engineering Services (Pvt) Limited, Colombo, Sri Lanka — subsidiary: Step-down subsidiary of MDL; 100% held by Colombo Dockyard PLC. Date of acquisition 19.01.2026; reporting currency LKR. Named 'DOCKYARD GENERAL ENGINEERING SERVICES LIMITED' in Form AOC-1 and 'Dockyard General Engineering Services (Pvt) Limited' in the Board's Report — the AR is internally inconsistent on the name. Activity not described in the routed text.
- Dockyard Total Solutions (Private) Limited, Colombo, Sri Lanka — subsidiary: Step-down subsidiary of MDL; 100% held by Colombo Dockyard PLC. Date of acquisition 19.01.2026; reporting currency LKR. Named 'DOCKYARD TOTAL SOLUTION (PRIVATE) LIMITED' in Form AOC-1 (singular 'SOLUTION') and 'Dockyard Total Solutions (Private) Limited' in the Board's Report. Activity not described in the routed text.
- Ceylon Shipping Agency (Pte) Limited, Singapore — subsidiary: Step-down subsidiary of MDL; 51% held by Colombo Dockyard PLC. Date of acquisition 19.01.2026; reporting currency SGD. Named 'CEYLON SHIPPING AGENCY (PRIVATE) LIMITED' in Form AOC-1 while the Board's Report gives 'Ceylon Shipping Agency (Pte) Limited, Singapore' — the AR is inconsistent on both the suffix and, implicitly, the jurisdiction. Activity not described in the routed text.
- Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) — associate: 47.21% held by MDL; the only associate company as at 31 March 2026. Date on which the associate was first acquired stated as 18 November 1967 (date of first acquisition of the shares). Significant influence arises through Voting Rights. Latest audited balance sheet date 31 March 2026. The RPT note records dividend received/receivable and states other transactions include rent and sales which are 'not significant in nature' — no amounts extracted.
- Ministry of Defence, Government of India — related party: Controlling Government entity and the principal customer. Disclosed under 'Government related entities where significant transactions carried out' with revenue from related party, amounts receivable/(payable) and dividend paid/payable columns — no amounts extracted. MDL has availed the Ind AS 24 exemption from detailed disclosure of transactions with Government and Government-related entities, so the RPT note is a partial disclosure by design.
- Key Managerial Personnel (Functional Directors, Company Secretary and Part-Time Non-Official Directors) — related party: Disclosed as related parties with short-term employee benefits, post-employment benefits and sitting fees. Named individuals include Capt. Jagmohan, Shri Biju George, Cdr. Vasudev Puranik, Shri Shailesh Bhalachandra Jamgaonkar, Shri Ruchir Agrawal, Shri Lalatendu Acharya, Smt. Madhavi Kulkarni, Shri Sanjeev Singhal (Retd., Director Finance upto 28.02.2025), Cdr. Jasbir Singh IN (Retd., Director S&HE upto 31.10.2024), and Independent Directors Shri Dattaprasad Prabhakar Kholkar, Shri Chandu Sambasiva Rao, Dr. Vivek Atul Bhuskute, Shri Kedar Nath Gupta, Smt. Veni Thapar, Shri Mallikarjunarao Bhyrishetty (upto 23.12.2024) and Smt. Neeru Singh Jagjeet Kaur (upto 23.02.2023). No remuneration amounts extracted. A stated finding: loans or advances in the nature of loans granted to promoters, directors, KMPs and related parties, severally or jointly, are Nil (Previous Year: Nil).

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Warships for the Indian Navy:** Project P15B Visakhapatnam Class Guided Missile Destroyers (all four delivered ahead of contractual schedule), Project P17A Nilgiri Class Stealth Frigates (INS Nilgiri, INS Udaygiri, INS Taragiri, INS Mahendragiri), Destroyers, frigates, corvettes, missile boats and offshore patrol vessels delivered since nationalisation in 1960
- **Submarines and submarine lifecycle support:** Project P-75 Scorpene Class conventional submarines built under licence with French collaborator M/s Naval Group (six delivered, including INS Kalvari and INS Vaghsheer), German SSK Class submarines (INS Shalki, first Indian-built submarine), R&D programmes for Expendable Underwater Target and Mobile Target Emulator, Global submarine lifecycle support across both SSK and Scorpene technologies
- **Indian Coast Guard vessels:** Training Ship (1), Next Generation Offshore Patrol Vessels (6), Fast Patrol Vessels (14)
- **Export commercial vessels:** 7,500 DWT Multi-Purpose Hybrid Powered Vessels for Navi Merchants A/S, Denmark (six, with an option for four more)
- **Green vessels:** Methanol Dual Fuel Diesel Electric Platform Supply Vessel (3,000 DWT) for the Shipping Corporation of India — described as India's first
- **Offshore projects:** ONGC Part Replacement of Pipeline Project (PRPP) — subsea pipelines, approx. 44 km, ONGC Discovered Small Field-II — six new wellhead platforms, modification of three platforms, subsea pipe laying approx. 200 km, ONGC PRP 8(a) — subsea pipe laying approx. 59.8 km plus 17.9 km piggyback with modification to existing platforms
- **Ship repair and refit:** Repair, refit, maintenance and modernisation of defence and commercial vessels, Coast Guard vessel refit and guarantee support (ICGS Saksham)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Continuous modernisation of naval assets and strengthening of maritime capabilities are expected to drive sustained demand for warships, submarines, support vessels, specialised platforms and lifecycle support services.
- Government policy — Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Make in India / Make for the World, the Defence Acquisition Procedure, positive indigenisation lists and increasing emphasis on domestic procurement — is stated to be creating significant opportunities for Indian defence manufacturers and shipyards.
- India's reassessed coastline of 11,098.81 kilometres and location along major international shipping routes are cited as the foundation for a robust maritime ecosystem; maritime trade is expected to grow in line with economic expansion.
- Ship repair and lifecycle support services are expected to emerge as an important growth driver in the coming years, driven by the expanding fleet of defence and commercial vessels requiring maintenance, modernisation and operational support.
- Government focus on maritime infrastructure, port-led development, coastal shipping and the blue economy is expected to strengthen growth prospects for shipbuilding, ship repair and marine engineering.
- Increasing capital expenditure on defence modernisation and growing participation of domestic industry are stated to be structurally transforming India's defence manufacturing sector.
- Margin watch-item: cost escalation, inflationary pressures, foreign exchange volatility and execution delays may adversely affect margins under fixed-price contracts, particularly where imported equipment, systems and critical material are involved.
- Competitive watch-item: growing participation of private sector entities and international players in defence manufacturing may intensify competition for future business opportunities.
- Execution-cycle constraint: warship and submarine construction involves extended execution timelines owing to technological complexity, stringent quality requirements and evolving customer specifications.
- Structural constraint acknowledged: certain critical systems, sensors, propulsion equipment and specialised components continue to be sourced from overseas suppliers, exposing the Company to supply chain and geopolitical risk.
- Operating constraint acknowledged: waterfront operations require periodic dredging and maintenance, involving recurring expenditure and operational planning challenges.
- Outstanding order book as at 31 March 2026 stood at Rs 20,535 crore, spanning defence warships, submarines, Coast Guard vessels, offshore EPC, export commercial vessels and India's first green methanol Platform Supply Vessel.
- Order book as at 31 March 2025 was Rs 32,260 crore; the Company states the year-on-year reduction reflects the strength of its execution.
- At Rs 20,535 crore as on 31 March 2026, the order book is stated to represent approximately 1.6 times annual revenue, providing multi-year forward visibility.
- Coast Guard Projects — 1 Training Ship, 6 Next Generation Offshore Patrol Vessels and 14 Fast Patrol Vessels (21 vessels under concurrent construction), contracts signed in October 2023, December 2023 and January 2024, total contract value Rs 2,991 crore.
- Export commercial vessels — order from M/s Navi Merchants, Denmark for six 7,500 DWT Multi-Purpose Hybrid Powered Vessels at USD 85 million (Rs 715 crore), with an optional clause for four more vessels.
- Green vessel — India's first Methanol Dual Fuel Diesel Electric Platform Supply Vessel for the Shipping Corporation of India, 3,000 DWT, Rs 365 crore.
- Offshore — three concurrent ONGC contracts (PRPP, DSF-II and PRP 8(a)) at a total value of Rs 7,597 crore including taxes, with Rs 3,320 crore balance remaining.
- Pipeline (not order book): the Company states it has historically maintained an order book worth tens of thousands of crores and names Project 75-I submarines and next-generation destroyers as major pipelines — an aspiration for future awards, not a booked order.
- The Board's Report states the Company 'maintained a robust order book during FY 2025-26, providing long-term revenue visibility' but the Board's Report section 2.2 as routed carries no total order-book figure — the Rs 20,535 crore figure comes from the Corporate Overview 'Financial Capital' spread.

margins.body: Q4 EBITDA margin dropped to 13.74% due to Rs.532cr provision on Denmark and Coast Guard FPV contracts (cost escalation from 2022-23 bid prices); fixed-price contracts dominate (2/3 of order book); raw material costs locked at bid stage; subcontracting costs up due to 27-ship parallel build and outsourcing; long-term margin upside from P-75(AS)/P-75(I) economies of scale

capital_allocation.body: Strong net cash position (Rs.11,000-12,000cr); no debt planned; focus on internal funding of CAPEX; potential for dividend payout or strategic M&A in ship repair/commercial segment

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: MDL's expansion programme is entirely infrastructure-led and is described as continuous upgradation and modernisation of existing facilities rather than a single named project. NHAVA YARD: development of the Company's land parcel at Nhava, admeasuring approximately 37 acres, is described as one of the most significant capacity expansion initiatives undertaken by the Company. The greenfield shipyard is being developed in a phased manner to support shipbuilding, ship repair and future growth; facilities include Hard Stands, a Jetty, Workshops, Stores, an Administrative Building, provision of LL Cranes and allied services, and will facilitate construction of ships and offshore platforms. The short-term development plan focuses on optimising utilisation of existing infrastructure to support current business opportunities; the long-term plan aims to establish world-class facilities capable of supporting construction, repair and modernisation of larger and more complex vessels and submarines. No completion date is stated. SOUTH YARD ANNEX / ADDITIONAL WATERFRONT INFRASTRUCTURE: development of a newly acquired land parcel of approximately 15 acres adjacent to the existing facilities (adjacent to MPA land) to enable simultaneous construction, outfitting and repair/refit of various types of vessels; on completion the AR states the project 'will enhance the waterfront handling capacity from the existing 80 DWT to 200 DWT, enabling simultaneous execution of multiple projects'. The unit 'DWT' is reproduced exactly as printed. No completion date is stated. FLOATING DRY DOCK: development of a new Floating Dry Dock of 12,000T capacity has been undertaken to handle the dry-docking requirements of future major projects and to improve docking flexibility and support growth in ship repair, maintenance and modernisation. No completion date is stated. CRANES AND YARD WORKS: replacement of the existing eight vintage Level Luffing Cranes with new modernised cranes is being undertaken in a phased manner (the Corporate Overview 'Financial Capital' spread states this programme is 65% complete); a 150 T Level Luffing Crane is being set up at Alcock Yard; a new Fabrication Workshop including stores is being set up at Alcock Yard; a new Caisson Gate is being manufactured for the East Yard Dry Dock to replace the existing gate; replacement of the Kasara Basin Gate is in progress; and infrastructure augmentation is being progressed in the East Yard to undertake pressure hull fabrication for future Submarine projects. FUTURE GREENFIELD SHIPYARD: the Company states it is in dialogue with State Governments (Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh) on both coasts of India to explore the feasibility of setting up a Greenfield Shipyard in line with the Government of India's Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 — a feasibility dialogue, not a sanctioned project. STATED AMBITION: the Value Creation Story spread states the capital expenditure programme includes acquiring adjacent land parcels to construct larger dry docks, 'aiming to nearly double its total shipbuilding and vessel repair capacities'. RUPEE QUANTUM (stated in prose, deliberately NOT placed in capex_disclosed because it does not arrive under a NAMED DISCLOSURE heading): the Corporate Overview 'Financial Capital' chapter states 'Capital expenditure for FY 2025-26 was Rs 471.81 crore, directed entirely at infrastructure modernisation: the phased crane replacement programme (65% complete), Nhava Yard development, the new 12,000T Floating Dry Dock, Alcock Yard infrastructure additions, and South Yard Annex preparation', and separately that MDL invested Rs 236.95 crore in the equity of Colombo Dockyard PLC, with all capex and the CDPLC investment self-funded from operating cashflows. OPERATIONAL CAPEX ADJACENCY: fabrication of two Jackets and Top sides for the ONGC DSF-II project at the Nhava Yard is approaching completion, with four more Jackets and Top sides in progress at Vietnam; ONGC PRP 8(a) pipe-laying is expected to be completed during the next season, spanning 15 October 2026 to 15 May 2027. TRUNCATION WARNING: the Board's Report section 2.4 'Other Infrastructure Projects' is cut off after its first clause ('Towards undertaking the construction of advanced and next generation vessels, MDL has undertaken') — an entire additional infrastructure list is missing from the routed text and is not recoverable from any sibling bundle.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Only Indian shipyard to have constructed both destroyers and conventional submarines for the Indian Navy — a unique position within India's defence manufacturing ecosystem
- Only Indian yard to have built both German SSK Class and French Scorpene Class submarines, and the only yard providing lifecycle support across both technologies
- Two completely independent submarine assembly and launch lines (stated in the Value Creation Story spread)
- Indigenous content in vessels built has risen from 42% in the P15 Delhi Class Destroyers of the 1990s to 75% in the P17A Nilgiri Class Frigates, with a large number of items indigenised through Indian industry, predominantly MSMEs
- Navratna Defence PSU status (conferred 2024 — first government-owned shipyard and third Defence PSU to receive it), operating under the administrative control of the Ministry of Defence
- Zero-debt enterprise with capital requirements fully met through internal accruals — capex and the Colombo Dockyard investment self-funded
- Proven delivery record: all four P15B destroyers delivered before contractual timelines; over 800 platforms built since 1960 including 31 capital warships and 8 submarines
- Strategic geographic location in Mumbai, headquarters of the Western Naval Command, giving proximity to customers, suppliers and ancillary industries
- Strong pool of naval architects, engineers, project professionals and technical specialists with design and systems-integration experience
- Portfolio breadth across eight product and service lines described as unique in India's shipbuilding landscape
- 250-year operating heritage (founded 1774; incorporated 1934; acquired by the Government of India in 1960)

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Delays in P-75(AS)/P-75(I) contract signing; cost overruns in fixed-price contracts; supply chain disruptions for imported components; geopolitical delays in RFPs (P-17B, MCMV); labor and skill shortages; provision reversals uncertain

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Rs.3,700cr P-15B and Rs.2,700cr P-75 backlog are not revenue but guarantee/liability provisions; Rs.4,000cr ship repair revenue includes AIP/MRLC upgrades (not dry dock repairs); Rs.6,500cr ONGC order is offshore support vessel (not oil rigs); submarine CAPEX is for indigenous assembly, not nuclear

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Strengthen its position as India's premier defence shipyard while pursuing diversification, infrastructure expansion, operational excellence and international growth.
- Build ship repair, refit and lifecycle support into a major vertical — the Company states it accords strategic importance to this segment and is undertaking initiatives to expand its repair and refit capabilities.
